drills.q: What sits between the emulator and your program?
options: The line discipline, which is kernel code
Nothing; they are connected directly
A library in your process
The shell
drills.why: It holds a buffer, edits it, echoes it, and turns certain bytes into signals, and neither program did any of that.

drills.q: In canonical mode, when does a read return?
options: When a newline reaches the buffer
As soon as any byte arrives
After a short timeout
When the buffer is full
drills.why: Which is why a program asking for one keypress appears to hang. The key was delivered and it is waiting in a kernel buffer.

drills.q: Why does backspace work before your program runs?
options: The discipline holds the line and can take a character back off it
The emulator deletes the character locally
The shell intercepts it
The keyboard sends a correction sequence
drills.why: And on this machine the byte it treats as erase is 0x7f, which is delete rather than backspace.

drills.q: A pseudoterminal with no process attached receives four bytes of input. What comes back?
options: Four bytes, because ECHO is set and echo does not need a reader
Nothing, because nothing is reading
Nothing, because nothing printed them
Four bytes, but only after a program attaches
drills.why: Measured directly: write abc and a newline into the master and read back abc, a carriage return, and a newline, with no program in the picture.

drills.q: How does a program stop a password appearing on screen?
options: It clears ECHO, reads, and sets it back
It avoids printing what it read
It writes spaces over the characters
It reads from a different descriptor
drills.why: It was never printing the password. If it crashes between clearing and restoring, your shell stays silent until you fix the flag by hand.

drills.q: The Enter key sends 0x0D. What does your program read by default?
options: 0x0A, because ICRNL translates it
0x0D
Both bytes
Whichever the emulator was configured for
drills.why: The terminal speaks carriage return and the program speaks newline, and the kernel translates in both directions without either one knowing.

drills.q: A program writes five bytes ending in a newline. How many reach the terminal?
options: Six, because ONLCR expands it
Five
Six, but only if the program asked for it
It depends on the emulator
drills.why: And turning the output translation off is what produces the staircase, where every line starts where the previous one ended.

drills.q: Which flag has to be set for ONLCR to do anything?
options: OPOST
ICANON
ISIG
IEXTEN
drills.why: Raw mode clears OPOST, so the expansion stops even though ONLCR itself is still set, which is what a raw pseudoterminal reports when measured.

drills.q: What is special about the byte 0x03 to the hardware?
options: Nothing; a flag and a table decide what happens to it
The keyboard controller raises an interrupt for it
The CPU treats it as a trap
It is delivered on a separate channel
drills.why: With ISIG set, a child reading a terminal dies of signal 2 when it arrives. With ISIG clear, the same child reads a byte with value 3.

drills.q: Ctrl-C does nothing in an editor. What is the most likely reason?
options: The program cleared ISIG, so it receives the byte
The emulator did not send anything
The signal cannot reach a program in the foreground
The terminal was in canonical mode
drills.why: The other possibility is that the signal arrived correctly and the program ignores SIGINT, which looks identical from outside.

options: A name for clearing ICANON, ECHO, ISIG, ICRNL and OPOST together
A separate mode in the kernel driver
A mode where the emulator stops interpreting bytes
Direct access to the keyboard device
drills.why: There is no raw bit. The convenience function clears a set of flags, and every consequence follows from which ones.

drills.q: What does a program owe the terminal once it is in raw mode?
options: Echoing, line editing, interpreting 0x03, and emitting carriage returns
Nothing extra; the kernel still handles those
Only echoing
Restoring the flags, and nothing else
drills.why: That is the deal: every keystroke the instant it arrives, in exchange for doing the discipline's work yourself.

drills.q: VMIN and VTIME default to one and zero. What does that mean?
options: Return as soon as one byte exists, and never time out
Return after one tenth of a second
Return when one byte exists or a tenth of a second passes
Block until at least one byte and one tenth of a second
drills.why: A VTIME of zero is no timer at all rather than a timer that already expired, which is why a read with nothing available blocks.

drills.q: What are VMIN and VTIME actually used for in a full-screen program?
options: Telling an escape key pressed alone from an escape sequence still arriving
Throttling how fast input is processed
Setting the repeat rate
Batching writes to the screen
drills.why: A tenth of a second is long enough for the rest of a sequence and short enough that a lone escape key does not feel stuck.

drills.q: Where does the window size live?
options: In the kernel device, readable from either end
In an environment variable
In the emulator only
In the shell's memory
drills.why: A fresh pseudoterminal measures zero by zero. Set 40 by 132 on the master and the slave reads 40 by 132, because there is one pair of numbers.
